danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Da Pierre vendte hjem fra sin rejse gennem det sydlige Rusland i det lykkeligste sindsstemning, opfyldte han et længe næret forsæt om at besøge sin ven Bolkonskij (fyrst Andrej), som han ikke havde set i to år.

Bogutjarovo lå i en flad, kedelig egn af landet blandt marker og skove af gran og birk, der delvist var fældet. Huset lå bag en nygravet dam, fyldt til randen med vand og med bredder, der endnu var uden græs. Det lå for enden af en landsby, der strakte sig langs landevejen, midt i en ung lund med nogle få grantræer.

Gårdanlægget bestod af en tærskeplads, udhuse, stalde, et badehus, et porthus og et stort murstenshus med halvrund facade, der stadig var under opførelse. Rundt om huset var en nyanlagt have. Hegn og porte var nye og solide; to brandsprøjter og en vandvogn, malet grøn, stod i et skur; stierne var lige, broerne var stærke og havde gelændere. Alt bar præg af orden og god forvaltning. Nogle huslivegne, Pierre mødte, svarede på hans forespørgsler om, hvor fyrsten boede, ved at pege på et lille, nybygget hus tæt ved dammen. Anton, en mand, der havde passet fyrst Andrej i hans barndom, hjalp Pierre ud af vognen, sagde, at fyrsten var hjemme, og viste ham ind i en ren, lille forstue.
Pierre blev slået af det lille, beskedne, men rene hus sammenlignet med de strålende omgivelser, hvori han sidst havde mødt sin ven i Petersborg.
Han gik med raske skridt ind i den lille modtagelsesstue med dens endnu upudsede bræddevægge, der duftede af fyr, og ville gå videre, men Anton løb foran på tåspidser og bankede på en dør.
»Nå, hvad er det?« lød en skarp, ubehagelig stemme.
»En gæst,« svarede Anton.
»Bed ham vente,« og man hørte lyden af en stol, der blev skubbet tilbage.

Pierre gik med raske skridt til døren og stod pludselig ansigt til ansigt med fyrst Andrej, der kom ud med rynket pande og så ældet ud. Pierre omfavnede ham, løftede sine briller og kyssede sin ven på kinden og betragtede ham nøje.
»Nå, det havde jeg ikke ventet — jeg er meget glad,« sagde fyrst Andrej.

Pierre sagde intet; han betragtede blot sin ven med overraskelse. Han var slået af forandringen i ham. Hans ord var venlige, og der var et smil på hans læber og i hans ansigt, men hans øjne var sløve og livløse, og trods hans tydelige ønske om det kunne han ikke give dem et glad og lystigt glimt. Fyrst Andrej var blevet tyndere, blegere og mere mandigt, men det, der forbløffede og distancerede Pierre, indtil han vænnede sig til det, var hans sløvhed og en rynke i panden, der tydede på langvarig fordybelse i én eneste tanke.

Som det sædvanligvis sker, når mennesker mødes efter en langvarig adskillelse, var det længe, før deres samtale fandt fodfæste. De stillede spørgsmål og gav korte svar om ting, de vidste burde drøftes udførligt. Omsider gled samtalen gradvis ind på nogle af de emner, der først kun var let berørt: deres fortidige liv, planer for fremtiden, Pierres rejser og beskæftigelser, krigen og så videre. Den optagethed og mismodighed, Pierre havde bemærket i sin vens blik, var nu endnu tydeligere i det smil, hvormed han lyttede til Pierre, især når denne talte med glad begejstring om fortid eller fremtid. Det var, som om fyrst Andrej gerne ville have delt Pierres begejstring, men ikke kunne. Pierre begyndte at føle, at det var i dårlig smag at tale om sine forhåbninger, drømme og forventninger om lykke eller godhed i fyrst Andrejs nærværelse. Han skammede sig over at udtrykke sine nye frimuriske synspunkter, der var blevet særlig fornyet og styrket af hans nylige rejse. Han beherskede sig af frygt for at virke naiv, men følte dog en uimodståelig trang til hurtigst muligt at vise sin ven, at han nu var en helt anden og bedre Pierre end den, han havde været i Petersborg.
»Jeg kan ikke fortælle dig, hvor meget jeg har oplevet siden da. Jeg kender næppe mig selv igen.«
»Ja, vi har forandret os meget, meget meget, siden da,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
»Nå, og hvad med dig? Hvad er dine planer?«
»Planer!« gentog fyrst Andrej ironisk. »Mine planer?« sagde han, som forbavset over ordet. »Jamen, du kan se, jeg bygger. Jeg agter at bosætte mig her for alvor til næste år ...«
Pierre så tavst og spørgende ind i fyrst Andrejs ansigt, der var blevet meget ældre.
»Nej, det var ikke det, jeg mente ...« begyndte Pierre, men fyrst Andrej afbrød ham.
»Men hvorfor tale om mig? ... Fortæl mig, ja, fortæl mig om dine rejser og alt, hvad du har foretaget dig på dine godser.«

Pierre begyndte at fortælle om, hvad han havde gjort på sine godser, og forsøgte så vidt muligt at skjule sin egen andel i de forbedringer, der var sket. Fyrst Andrej ansporede flere gange Pierres beretning om, hvad han havde gjort, som om det hele var en gammel historie, og han lyttede ikke blot uden interesse, men endda som om han skammede sig over det, Pierre fortalte ham.
Pierre følte sig ilde til mode og ligefrem nedtrykt i sin vens selskab og blev til sidst tavs.

»Hør, min kære ven,« sagde fyrst Andrej, der tydeligvis også følte sig nedtrykt og utilpas med sin gæst, »jeg er kun her på gennemrejse og er lige kommet for at se til tingene. Jeg tager tilbage til min søster i dag. Jeg vil præsentere dig for hende. Men du kender hende jo allerede,« sagde han, tydeligvis forsøgende at underholde en gæst, med hvem han nu ikke fandt noget fælles. »Vi tager efter middag. Og vil du nu se dig lidt om?«

De gik ud og spadserede rundt til middagstid, mens de talte om politiske nyheder og fælles bekendte, som mennesker der ikke kender hinanden intimt. Fyrst Andrej talte med nogen iver og interesse kun om den nye gård, han var ved at opføre, og dens bygninger, men selv dér, mens de stod på stilladset midt i en snak om husets fremtidige indretning, afbrød han sig selv:
»Nå, men det er slet ikke interessant. Lad os spise, og så tager vi af sted.«
Ved middagen drejede samtalen sig om Pierres ægteskab.
»Jeg blev meget overrasket, da jeg hørte om det,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
Pierre rødmede, som han altid gjorde, når det blev nævnt, og sagde hastigt: »Jeg fortæller dig engang, hvordan det hele gik til. Men du ved, det er forbi, og for altid.«
»For altid?« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Intet er for altid.«
»Men du ved, hvordan det endte, gør du ikke? Du har hørt om duellen?«
»Ja, også det måtte du igennem!«
»Én ting takker jeg Gud for — at jeg ikke slog det menneske ihjel,« sagde Pierre.
»Hvorfor det?« spurgte fyrst Andrej. »At slå en ondskabsfuld hund ihjel er en rigtig god ting i virkeligheden.«
»Nej, at slå et menneske ihjel er dårligt — forkert.«

»Hvorfor er det forkert?« insisterede fyrst Andrej. »Det er ikke givet mennesket at vide, hvad der er rigtigt, og hvad der er forkert. Mennesker har altid taget fejl og vil altid tage fejl, og i intet mere end i, hvad de anser for rigtigt og forkert.«

»Det, der skader en anden, er forkert,« sagde Pierre og følte med tilfredshed, at fyrst Andrej for første gang siden hans ankomst var vakt, var begyndt at tale og ønskede at udtrykke det, der havde bragt ham til hans nuværende tilstand.
»Og hvem har fortalt dig, hvad der er skadeligt for et andet menneske?« spurgte han.
»Skadeligt! Skadeligt!« udbrød Pierre. »Vi ved alle, hvad der er skadeligt for os selv.«

»Ja, det ved vi, men den skade, jeg er bevidst om i mig selv, er noget, jeg ikke kan tilføje andre,« sagde fyrst Andrej, stadig mere ivrig og tydeligvis ønskende at udtrykke sit nye livssyn for Pierre. Han talte på fransk. »Jeg kender kun to virkelige onder i livet: anger og sygdom. Det eneste gode er fraværet af disse onder. At leve for mig selv og undgå disse to onder er hele min livsfilosofi nu.«

»Og kærlighed til sin næste og selvopofrelse?« begyndte Pierre. »Nej, det kan jeg ikke gå med til! At leve blot for ikke at gøre ondt og ikke behøve at fortryde er ikke nok. Jeg levede sådan, jeg levede for mig selv og ødelagde mit liv. Og først nu, da jeg lever, eller i det mindste forsøger« (Pierres beskedenhed fik ham til at rette sig selv) »at leve for andre, først nu har jeg forstået al livets lykke. Nej, jeg kan ikke give dig ret, og det tror du heller ikke selv.« Fyrst Andrej så tavst på Pierre med et ironisk smil.

»Når du møder min søster, fyrstinde Marja, vil I komme godt ud af det,« sagde han. »Måske har du ret for dit eget vedkommende,« tilføjede han efter en kort pause, »men enhver lever på sin måde. Du levede for dig selv og siger, at du næsten ødelagde dit liv, og først fandt lykke, da du begyndte at leve for andre. Jeg oplevede det stik modsatte. Jeg levede for ære — og hvad er ære i grunden? Den samme kærlighed til andre, et ønske om at gøre noget for dem, et ønske om deres bifald. Jeg levede altså for andre og ødelagde ikke næsten, men fuldstændig mit liv. Og jeg er blevet roligere, siden jeg begyndte at leve kun for mig selv.«
»Men hvad mener du med at leve kun for dig selv?« spurgte Pierre og blev ivrig. »Hvad med din søn, din søster og din far?«

»Men det er jo det samme som mig selv — de er ikke andre,« forklarede fyrst Andrej. »De andre, ens næste, le prochain, som du og fyrstinde Marja kalder det, er den vigtigste kilde til al fejl og alt ondt. Le prochain — dine bønder i Kiev, som du ønsker at gøre godt for.«
Og han så på Pierre med et spottende, udfordrende udtryk. Han ønskede tydeligvis at lokke ham.

»Du spøger,« svarede Pierre og blev mere og mere ivrig. »Hvad fejl eller ondt kan der være i, at jeg ønsker at gøre godt, ja endda gør lidt — skønt jeg gjorde meget lidt og gjorde det meget dårligt? Hvad ondt kan der være i, at ulykkelige mennesker, vores livegne, mennesker som os selv, voksede op og døde uden nogen forestilling om Gud og sandhed ud over ceremonier og meningsløse bønner og nu undervises i en trøstende tro på et kommende liv, gengældelse, belønning og trøst? Hvad ondt og fejl er der i det, hvis mennesker døde af sygdom uden hjælp, mens materiel bistand så let kunne ydes, og jeg skaffede dem en læge, et hospital og et asyl for de gamle? Og er det ikke et håndgribeligt, uomtvisteligt gode, hvis en bonde eller en kvinde med et spædbarn ikke har hvile dag eller nat, og jeg giver dem hvile og fritid?« sagde Pierre hastigt og med udtalefejl. »Og det har jeg gjort, omend dårligt og i ringe omfang; men jeg har gjort noget i den retning, og du kan ikke overbevise mig om, at det ikke var en god handling, og mere end det — du kan ikke få mig til at tro, at du ikke selv mener det. Og det vigtigste er,« fortsatte han, »at jeg ved, og ved det med sikkerhed, at glæden ved at gøre dette godt er den eneste sikre lykke i livet.«

»Ja, hvis man stiller det op på den måde, er det en helt anden sag,« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Jeg bygger et hus og anlægger en have, og du bygger hospitaler. Det ene og det andet kan tjene som tidsfordriv. Men hvad der er rigtigt og godt, må bedømmes af den, der ved alt, ikke af os. Nå, du vil have en diskussion,« tilføjede han, »så kom an.«
De rejste sig fra bordet og satte sig i indgangspartiet, der tjente som veranda.

»Kom, lad os diskutere,« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Du taler om skoler,« fortsatte han og bøjede en finger, »uddannelse og så videre; det vil sige, du ønsker at løfte ham« (han pegede på en bonde, der gik forbi og tog sin kasket af) »op fra hans dyriske tilstand og vække åndelige behov i ham, mens det forekommer mig, at dyrisk lykke er den eneste mulige lykke, og det er netop den, du vil berøve ham. Jeg misunder ham, men du vil gøre ham til, hvad jeg er, uden at give ham mine midler. Så siger du: 'let hans slid.' Men som jeg ser det, er fysisk arbejde lige så nødvendigt for ham, lige så stor en betingelse for hans eksistens, som åndeligt arbejde er for dig eller mig. Du kan ikke lade være med at tænke. Jeg går i seng efter klokken to om natten, tankerne kommer, og jeg kan ikke sove, men vælter mig rundt til daggry, fordi jeg tænker og ikke kan lade være — præcis som han ikke kan lade være med at pløje og meje; gjorde han det ikke, ville han gå på kro eller blive syg. Ligesom jeg ikke kunne udholde hans forfærdelige fysiske slid, men ville dø af det i løbet af en uge, kunne han ikke udholde min fysiske lediggang, men ville blive fed og dø. Det tredje — hvad var det nu, du talte om?« og fyrst Andrej bøjede en tredje finger. »Nå ja, hospitaler, medicin. Han får et anfald, han er døende, og du kommer og årelader ham og lapper ham sammen. Han slæber sig af sted som krøbling, en byrde for alle, i ti år mere. Det ville være langt lettere og enklere for ham at dø. Andre fødes, og der er rigeligt af dem i forvejen. Det ville være en anden sag, hvis du nødigt mistede en arbejder — det er sådan, jeg ser på ham — men du vil helbrede ham af kærlighed til ham. Og han ønsker det ikke. Og desuden — den forestilling, at medicin nogensinde har helbredt nogen! Slået dem ihjel, ja!« sagde han vredt og vendte sig fra Pierre.

Fyrst Andrej udtrykte sine idéer så klart og tydeligt, at det var åbenlyst, at han havde tænkt over dette emne mere end én gang, og han talte beredvilligt og hurtigt som en mand, der længe ikke har talt. Hans blik blev mere levende, jo mere håbløse hans konklusioner blev.

»Åh, det er forfærdeligt, forfærdeligt!« sagde Pierre. »Jeg forstår ikke, hvordan man kan leve med sådanne tanker. Jeg har selv haft sådanne øjeblikke for nylig, i Moskva og under mine rejser, men på sådanne tidspunkter bryder jeg sådan sammen, at jeg slet ikke lever — alting synes mig forhadt ... mig selv mest af alt. Så spiser jeg ikke, vasker mig ikke ... og hvordan er det med dig? ...«

»Hvorfor ikke vaske sig? Det er jo uhygiejnisk,« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Tværtimod bør man forsøge at gøre sit liv så behageligt som muligt. Jeg er i live, det er ikke min skyld, og altså må jeg leve mit liv så godt, jeg kan, uden at skade andre.«
»Men med sådanne tanker — hvad motiv har du da for at leve? Man ville sidde uden at røre sig, uden at foretage sig noget ...«

»Livet, som det er, lader én ingen fred. Jeg ville med glæde lade være med at foretage mig noget, men her har på den ene side den lokale adel gjort mig den ære at vælge mig til deres marskal; det var alt, jeg kunne gøre at komme ud af det. De kunne ikke forstå, at jeg mangler de nødvendige egenskaber — den slags godmodigt travl overfladiskhed, der er nødvendig for stillingen. Så er der dette hus, der skal bygges, for at man kan have en krog til sig selv, hvor man kan have ro. Og nu er der dette med udskrivningen.«
»Hvorfor gør du ikke tjeneste i hæren?«

»Efter Austerlitz!« sagde fyrst Andrej dystert. »Nej, mange tak! Jeg har lovet mig selv aldrig mere at gøre tjeneste i den aktive russiske hær. Det vil jeg ikke — heller ikke om Bonaparte stod her ved Smolensk og truede Lysye Gory — heller ikke da ville jeg gøre tjeneste i den russiske hær! Nå, som jeg sagde,« fortsatte han og genvandt fatningen, »nu er der denne udskrivning. Min far er øverstkommanderende for det tredje distrikt, og min eneste måde at undgå aktiv tjeneste på er at gøre tjeneste under ham.«
»Altså gør du tjeneste?«
»Det gør jeg.«
Han holdt en kort pause.
»Og hvorfor gør du det?«

»Af den grund: Min far er en af sin tids mest bemærkelsesværdige mænd. Men han er ved at blive gammel, og selv om han ikke er direkte grusom, har han en alt for energisk karakter. Han er så vant til ubegrænset magt, at han er frygtindgydende, og nu har han denne myndighed som øverstkommanderende for udskrivningen, tildelt af kejseren. Hvis jeg var kommet to timer for sent for fjorten dage siden, ville han have hængt en kasserer i Jukhnovna,« sagde fyrst Andrej med et smil. »Så jeg gør tjeneste, fordi det kun er mig, der har nogen indflydelse på min far, og af og til kan redde ham fra handlinger, der siden ville pine ham.«
»Nå, der kan du selv se!«

»Ja, men det er ikke, som du forestiller dig,« fortsatte fyrst Andrej. »Jeg nærede ikke, og nærer ikke, den mindste sympati for den slyngel af en kontorist, der havde stjålet støvler fra rekrutterne; jeg ville endda gerne have set ham hængt, men jeg havde ondt af min far — det er igen for min egen skyld.«
Fyrst Andrej blev mere og mere livlig. Hans øjne glitrede febrilsk, mens han forsøgte at bevise for Pierre, at der i hans handlinger ikke var noget ønske om at gøre sin næste godt.

»Så ønsker du at frigøre dine livegne,« fortsatte han, »det er en meget god ting, men ikke for dig — for jeg formoder ikke, du nogensinde har ladet nogen piske eller sendt nogen til Sibirien — og endnu mindre for dine livegne. Hvis de bliver slået, pisket eller sendt til Sibirien, er de vel ikke desto værre stillet. I Sibirien fører de det samme dyriske liv, og striberne på deres kroppe heler, og de er lige så lykkelige som før. Men det er en god ting for godsejerne, der går moralsk til grunde, bringer anger over sig selv, undertrykker denne anger og bliver hårdhjertede som følge af at kunne uddele straffe retmæssigt og uretmæssigt. Det er de mennesker, jeg har ondt af, og for deres skyld ønsker jeg at frigøre de livegne. Du har måske ikke set det, men jeg har set, hvordan gode mennesker, opdraget i disse traditioner med ubegrænset magt, med tiden, efterhånden som de bliver mere pirrelige, bliver grusomme og hårde, er bevidste om det, men ikke kan beherske sig og bliver mere og mere ulykkelige.«
Fyrst Andrej talte så alvorligt, at Pierre ikke kunne lade være med at tænke, at disse tanker var inspireret af fyrst Andrejs fars tilfælde.
Han svarede ikke.
»Så det er det, jeg beklager — menneskets værdighed, sjælefred, renhed — og ikke de livegnes rygge og pander, som, slå og barbér dem som du vil, altid forbliver de samme rygge og pander.«
»Nej, nej! Tusind gange nej! Jeg vil aldrig give dig ret,« sagde Pierre.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Returning from his tour of southern Russia in the happiest frame of mind, Pierre carried out an intention he had long had — visiting his friend Bolkonski, whom he hadn't seen in two years.

Bogucharovo lay in a flat, uninteresting stretch of country among fields and forests of fir and birch, partly cut down. The house stood behind a newly dug pond, filled to the brim, its banks still bare. It was at the end of a village that stretched along the highway, in the middle of a young copse dotted with a few fir trees.

The homestead consisted of a threshing floor, outbuildings, stables, a bathhouse, a lodge, and a large brick house with a semicircular facade, still under construction. Around it was a newly laid-out garden. The fences and gates were new and solid; two fire pumps and a water cart, painted green, stood in a shed; the paths were straight, the bridges strong and had handrails. Everything bore the stamp of tidiness and good management. Some household serfs Pierre met, in reply to his question about where the prince lived, pointed to a small, recently built lodge near the pond. Anton, the man who had looked after Prince Andrew since childhood, helped Pierre out of his carriage, said the prince was home, and showed him into a clean little anteroom.
Pierre was struck by the modesty of the small but clean house after the grand surroundings in which he had last seen his friend in Petersburg.
He quickly entered the little reception room with its still-unplastered wooden walls, fragrant with pine, and would have gone farther, but Anton ran ahead on tiptoe and knocked at a door.
"Well, what is it?" came a sharp, unpleasant voice.
"A visitor," Anton answered.
"Ask him to wait," and the sound of a chair being pushed back was heard.

Pierre walked quickly to the door and came face to face with Prince Andrew, who emerged frowning and looking older. Pierre embraced him and, lifting his spectacles, kissed his friend on the cheek and studied him closely.
"Well, I didn't expect you — but I'm very glad," said Prince Andrew.

Pierre said nothing; he stared at his friend in surprise. He was struck by the change in him. His words were kind and there was a smile on his lips, but his eyes were dull and lifeless, and despite an obvious wish to appear otherwise, he couldn't give them a joyful, glad sparkle. Prince Andrew had grown thinner, paler, and more manly, but what startled and estranged Pierre — until he got used to it — were his apathy and a deep crease on his brow, the mark of prolonged concentration on a single thought.

As usually happens when people meet after a long separation, their conversation was slow to settle on anything. They asked questions and gave brief answers about topics they knew should be discussed at length. Eventually the talk gradually found its footing, touching on their past, their plans, Pierre's travels and activities, the war, and so on. The preoccupation and gloom Pierre had noticed in his friend's expression were now even more evident in the smile with which he listened — especially when Pierre spoke with happy excitement about the past or the future. It was as if Prince Andrew wanted to sympathize with what Pierre was saying but couldn't. Pierre began to feel it was in poor taste to talk about his enthusiasms, dreams, and hopes for happiness in Prince Andrew's presence. He was embarrassed to share his new Masonic views, which his recent travels had especially strengthened. He held himself back, afraid of seeming naive; and yet he felt an irresistible desire to show his friend as soon as possible that he was now a completely different and better Pierre than the one Prince Andrew had known in Petersburg.
"I can't tell you how much I've lived through since then. I hardly recognize myself."
"Yes, we've changed a great deal — very much — since then," said Prince Andrew.
"Well, and you? What are your plans?"
"Plans!" Prince Andrew repeated ironically. "My plans?" he said, as though astonished by the word. "Well, you see, I'm building. I plan to settle here for good next year..."
Pierre looked silently and searchingly into Prince Andrew's face, which had aged considerably.
"No, I meant to ask..." Pierre began, but Prince Andrew interrupted.
"But why talk about me? Tell me about yourself — about your travels and everything you've been doing on your estates."

Pierre began describing what he had done on his estates, trying as much as possible to downplay his own role in the improvements. Prince Andrew several times prompted Pierre's account, as though it were all an old, familiar story, and he listened not only without interest but as if embarrassed by what Pierre was telling him.
Pierre began to feel uncomfortable and even depressed in his friend's company, and at last fell silent.

"I'll tell you what, my dear fellow," said Prince Andrew — who also clearly felt awkward and constrained with his visitor — "I'm only camping out here and just came to look things over. I'm going back to my sister today. I'll introduce you to her. Though of course you know her already," he added, obviously trying to entertain a guest with whom he now had nothing in common. "We'll go after dinner. And would you like to look around the place now?"

They went out and walked about until dinnertime, talking about political news and mutual acquaintances like people who aren't close. Prince Andrew spoke with some energy and interest only about the new house and its construction; but even then, while standing on the scaffolding in the middle of explaining the future layout, he suddenly broke off:
"Anyway, this isn't interesting at all. Let's have dinner, and then we'll set off."
At dinner the conversation turned to Pierre's marriage.
"I was very surprised when I heard about it," said Prince Andrew.
Pierre blushed, as he always did when the subject came up, and said hurriedly: "I'll tell you someday how it all happened. But you know it's over — and forever."
"Forever?" said Prince Andrew. "Nothing is forever."
"But you know how it ended, don't you? You heard about the duel?"
"Yes, so you had to go through that too!"
"One thing I thank God for is that I didn't kill that man," said Pierre.
"Why?" asked Prince Andrew. "Killing a vicious dog is actually a good thing."
"No, killing a man is wrong — it's bad."

"Why is it wrong?" pressed Prince Andrew. "It's not given to us to know what is right and what is wrong. People always have erred and always will — and in nothing more than in what they consider right and wrong."

"What harms another person is wrong," said Pierre, pleased that for the first time since his arrival Prince Andrew was engaged, had started talking, and wanted to express what had brought him to his present state.
"And who told you what is harmful to another person?" Andrew asked.
"Bad! Bad!" exclaimed Pierre. "We all know what is bad for ourselves."

"Yes, we know that — but the harm I'm aware of in myself is something I can't inflict on others," said Prince Andrew, becoming more and more animated, clearly wanting to express his new outlook to Pierre. He switched to French. "I know only two very real evils in life: remorse and illness. The only good is the absence of those evils. To live for myself, avoiding those two evils — that's my whole philosophy now."

"And love of one's neighbor? And self-sacrifice?" Pierre began. "No, I can't agree with you! To live only so as not to do evil and not to feel regret — that's not enough. I lived like that once, I lived for myself and ruined my life. Only now, when I'm living — or at least trying" — Pierre's modesty made him correct himself — "to live for others, only now have I understood true happiness. No, I can't agree, and you don't really believe what you're saying." Prince Andrew looked at Pierre silently with an ironic smile.

"When you meet my sister — Princess Mary — you'll get along with her," he said. "Perhaps you're right, for yourself," he added after a short pause, "but everyone lives in his own way. You lived for yourself and say you nearly ruined your life and only found happiness when you started living for others. I had just the opposite experience. I lived for glory — and after all, what is glory? The same love of others, a desire to do something for them, a desire for their approval. So I lived for others, and not almost but completely ruined my life. And I've only found some peace since I began living for myself alone."
"But what do you mean by living for yourself alone?" asked Pierre, growing excited. "What about your son, your sister, your father?"

"But that's just the same as myself — they're not others," Prince Andrew explained. "Other people, one's neighbors — le prochain, as you and Princess Mary call it — are the main source of all error and evil. Le prochain — your Kiev peasants you want to do good for."
And he looked at Pierre with a mocking, challenging expression, clearly wanting to draw him out.

"You're joking," replied Pierre, growing more excited. "What error or evil can there be in my wishing to do good — and even doing a little, though I did it badly? What harm is there if unfortunate people — our serfs, people like us — were growing up and dying with no idea of God or truth beyond ceremonies and meaningless prayers, and are now learning a comforting faith in a future life, in retribution, reward, and consolation? What evil is there in providing a doctor, a hospital, and an asylum for the elderly to people who were dying of disease without any help, when such assistance is so easy to give? Isn't it an obvious, undeniable good to give rest and relief to a peasant or a mother with a baby who has no peace day or night?" said Pierre, speaking quickly, with a lisp. "And I've done that — though badly and in small measure — but I have done something, and you can't persuade me it wasn't a good thing. More than that, you can't make me believe you don't think so yourself. And the main thing," he went on, "is that I know — I know for certain — that the joy of doing good is the only sure happiness in life."

"Yes, if you put it that way, it's a different matter entirely," said Prince Andrew. "I build a house and plant a garden, and you build hospitals. Either one can serve as a pastime. But what's truly right and good can only be judged by someone who knows everything — not by us. Well, you want an argument," he added. "Come on, then."
They rose from the table and sat down in the entrance porch, which served as a veranda.

"Let's argue, then," said Prince Andrew. "You talk about schools," he went on, bending a finger, "education and the like — that is, you want to raise him" — he pointed to a peasant passing by who doffed his cap — "out of his animal condition and awaken spiritual needs in him. But it seems to me that animal happiness is the only happiness possible — and that's exactly what you want to take from him. I envy him, but you want to make him into what I am without giving him my resources. Then you say 'lighten his toil.' But as I see it, physical labor is as essential to him, as much a condition of his existence, as mental activity is to you or me. You can't help thinking. I go to bed after two in the morning, thoughts come, and I can't sleep — I toss until dawn because I think and can't stop, just as he can't stop plowing and mowing. If he didn't, he'd go to the tavern or fall sick. Just as I couldn't stand his terrible physical labor and would die within a week, he couldn't stand my idleness — he'd grow fat and die. And the third thing — what else did you mention?" He bent a third finger. "Ah, yes — hospitals, medicine. He has a seizure, he's dying, and you come along and bleed him and patch him up. He'll drag on as a cripple, a burden to everyone, for another ten years. It would be far easier and simpler for him to die. Others are being born — there are plenty as it is. It would be different if you were reluctant to lose a laborer — that's how I see him — but you want to cure him out of love. And he doesn't want that. Besides, what an idea — that medicine ever cured anyone! Killed them, yes!" he said, frowning angrily and turning away from Pierre.

Prince Andrew expressed his views so clearly and precisely that it was obvious he had thought about this at length. He spoke readily and rapidly, like a man who has not talked in a long time. His eyes grew more animated as his conclusions grew more bleak.

"Oh, that's terrible, terrible!" said Pierre. "I can't understand how one can live with such ideas. I had moments like that myself not long ago — in Moscow and while traveling — but at those times I collapsed so completely that I couldn't function, everything seemed hateful to me, myself most of all. Then I couldn't eat, couldn't wash... How is it with you?"

"Why not wash? That's unhygienic," said Prince Andrew. "On the contrary, one should try to make one's life as pleasant as possible. I'm alive — that's not my fault — so I must live out my life as best I can without hurting others."
"But with such views, what motive is there to go on living? One would just sit without moving, doing nothing..."

"Life itself doesn't leave you in peace. I'd be grateful to do nothing, but here on one hand the local nobility have done me the honor of electing me their marshal — I could barely get out of it. They couldn't understand that I lack the necessary qualities — the good-natured, fussy shallowness the job requires. Then there's this house, which has to be built to have a corner of my own for some peace. And now there's the recruiting."
"Why aren't you serving in the army?"

"After Austerlitz!" said Prince Andrew darkly. "No, thank you. I've promised myself never to serve in the active Russian army again. Not even if Bonaparte were here at Smolensk, threatening Bald Hills. Well, as I was saying," he continued, regaining his composure, "now there's the recruiting. My father is chief of the Third District, and my only way of avoiding active service is to serve under him."
"So you are serving?"
"I am."
He was quiet for a moment.
"And why do you serve?"

"For this reason: my father is one of the most remarkable men of his time. But he's growing old, and though not exactly cruel, he has too forceful a temperament. He's so accustomed to unlimited power that he's terrifying, and now he has this authority as a commander in chief of recruitment, granted by the Emperor. If I had been two hours late a couple of weeks ago, he would have had a paymaster's clerk at Yukhnovo hanged," said Prince Andrew with a smile. "So I serve because I'm the only one who has any influence over my father, and now and then I can save him from actions that would torment him afterward."
"Well, there you see!"

"Yes, but it's not the way you think," Prince Andrew continued. "I didn't and don't in the least care about that scoundrel of a clerk who stole boots from the recruits — I would actually have been glad to see him hanged. But I was sorry for my father — and that again is for my own sake."
Prince Andrew grew more and more animated. His eyes glittered feverishly as he tried to prove to Pierre that his actions contained no desire to do good for his neighbor.

"So — you want to liberate your serfs," he continued. "That's a very fine thing, but not for you — I don't suppose you've ever had anyone flogged or sent to Siberia — and still less for your serfs. If they're beaten, flogged, or sent to Siberia, I doubt they're any the worse for it. In Siberia they lead the same animal life, and the welts on their bodies heal, and they're as contented as before. But it's a good thing for the proprietors — who are destroyed morally, who bring remorse upon themselves, stifle that remorse, and grow callous as a result of having the power to punish justly and unjustly. It's those people I pity, and for their sake I would like to liberate the serfs. You may not have seen it, but I have — how good men raised in those traditions of unlimited power, as they grow more irritable with age, become cruel and harsh, know it, but can't control themselves, and grow more and more wretched."
Prince Andrew spoke so passionately that Pierre couldn't help thinking these ideas had been suggested by Prince Andrew's own father's case.
He said nothing in reply.
"So that's what I'm sorry for — human dignity, peace of mind, purity — and not the serfs' backs and foreheads, which, beat and shave them as you might, always remain the same backs and foreheads."
"No, no! A thousand times no! I will never agree with you," said Pierre.
